params.title: Components
params.subtitle: Photoconductors, capacitors, transformers, regulators, SCRs and TRIACs, special diodes, transistors and LEDs, plus the turns-ratio math.

onScreen: Photoconductors to LEDs, plus transformer turns-ratio math
scenes.narration: This lesson walks through the components the Element 3 exam asks about. We'll start with photoconductive devices, then capacitors, transformers, voltage regulators and Zener diodes, SCRs, or silicon-controlled rectifiers, and TRIACs, special diodes, transistors, light-emitting diodes, or LEDs, and a few other devices. For each one you'll learn what it does, and we'll work the transformer turns-ratio problems step by step. First up: what light does to a semiconductor.

callouts.label: Probes on a photoresistor, a cell of photoconductive material
Meter set to read resistance in ohms
Light frees electrons as extra charge carriers: conductivity rises
Bright light: low resistance. Darkness: high resistance

onScreen: Bright light: low resistance; darkness: high resistance
scenes.narration: Here's a photoresistor, a small cell of photoconductive material, with a multimeter set to read its resistance in ohms. When light shines on photoconductive material, its conductivity increases, because the light frees electrons to act as extra charge carriers. In crystalline solids like this one, the photoconductive effect produces a noticeable change in the resistance of the solid. In bright light the reading falls to a low resistance. In darkness it climbs back to a high resistance.

onScreen: Photoconductive: conductivity up, junction resistance down
Photovoltaic: light turned directly into an EMF
scenes.narration: 2 effects sound alike, so let's separate them. The photoconductive effect is the increased conductivity of an illuminated semiconductor junction. When a photosensitive semiconductor junction is illuminated, the junction resistance decreases, because the light creates extra electron-hole pairs that carry current. Turning light directly into an EMF, an electromotive force, is the photovoltaic effect. That's a different process, so don't mix the 2 up on the exam.

onScreen: Output circuit driven by a photosensitive device
Signal crosses the gap as light
No electrical connection between input and output
scenes.narration: An optoisolator, also called an optocoupler, is an LED and a photosensitive device in one package. On the input side, the circuit drives the LED. On the output side, the circuit is driven by the photosensitive device. The LED's light shines across a small gap onto the photosensitive device. Because the signal crosses the gap as light, the input and output circuits have no electrical connection. So when you see an LED and a photosensitive device, think optoisolator, or optocoupler.

params.title: What sets a capacitor's capacitance
steps: ε: dielectric constant between the plates
Plate voltage and stored charge don't change C
params.answer: Plate spacing and dielectric constant set C

onScreen: Voltage and charge don't change it
scenes.narration: What determines the capacitance of a capacitor? The formula is C equals epsilon A over d. Epsilon is the dielectric constant of the material between the plates, A is the plate area, and d is the distance between the plates. The voltage on the plates and the amount of charge stored do not change the capacitance. So for the exam, capacitance is determined by the distance between the plates and the dielectric constant of the material between them.

callouts.label: Dashed line: a small variable capacitor decreases parasitic oscillations
It neutralizes: opposite-phase feedback cancels unwanted feedback
Component 2: a capacitor to ground, the signal ground
Low reactance at RF shunts the signal away; it blocks DC, so bias is kept

onScreen: Dashed line: small variable capacitor decreases parasitic oscillations
Low reactance at RF, blocks DC
scenes.narration: Figure 3C4 shows radio frequency, or RF, stages between an oscillator and a power amplifier. If a small variable capacitor were installed in place of the dashed line, it would decrease parasitic oscillations. It acts as a neutralizing capacitor, feeding back an opposite-phase signal that cancels unwanted feedback through the transistor. Now find component 2. It provides a signal ground. It's a capacitor to ground whose low reactance at RF shunts the signal away, while it blocks direct current, or DC, so the bias is undisturbed.

callouts.label: Capacitor 3: the bypass capacitor
Emitter to ground, across the 100 Ω emitter resistor
AC signal bypasses the resistor, so the stage keeps its gain
1 µF capacitor with a potentiometer: used to adjust tone
Reactance varies with frequency; the pot sets how much audio passes

onScreen: 1 µF capacitor and potentiometer: adjust tone
scenes.narration: In Figure 3C5, which capacitor is the bypass capacitor? Capacitor 3. It connects a transistor's emitter to ground, across the 100 ohm emitter resistor. The alternating current, or AC, signal bypasses that resistor, so the stage keeps its gain. Now the 1 microfarad capacitor. It's connected to a potentiometer that is used to adjust tone. The capacitor's reactance changes with frequency, so the pot sets how much of part of the audio range passes.

blocks.label: Stage 2
blocks.note: Its own DC bias, kept separate

onScreen: Stage 1 with its own DC bias
Coupling capacitor: blocks DC, passes AC
scenes.narration: What is the purpose of a coupling capacitor? It blocks direct current and passes alternating current. The reason is its reactance: X sub C equals 1 over 2 pi f C. At DC, X sub C is infinite, so no direct current gets through. At signal frequencies, X sub C is small, so the signal passes easily. That lets the capacitor carry the signal from one stage to the next while keeping their DC bias separate.

params.title: A capacitor in series with the primary
items: A capacitor is sometimes placed in series with a power transformer's primary
Purpose: to improve the power factor
Its reactance offsets part of the primary's inductive reactance
The current comes closer to in phase with the voltage

onScreen: Capacitor in series with the primary
Current closer to in phase with voltage
scenes.narration: Now transformers. A capacitor is sometimes placed in series with the primary of a power transformer. Why? To improve the power factor. The primary winding is a coil, so it has inductive reactance. The capacitor's reactance offsets part of that inductive reactance, bringing the current closer to in phase with the voltage. That's a better power factor.

params.title: Turns ratio sets the voltage ratio
steps: #24 wire size sets current, not the voltage ratio
params.answer: Step-up: more turns on the secondary

onScreen: E sub S = E sub P × N sub S / N sub P
Wire size sets current, not ratio
scenes.narration: Voltage ratio equals turns ratio, so the secondary voltage, E sub S, equals E sub P times N sub S over N sub P. A primary of 2250 turns on 120 volts AC, with a 500-turn secondary: 120 times 500 over 2250 is 26.7 volts, a step-down. Next, 20 volts on a primary of 200 turns, with a secondary of 500 turns of the same size wire: 20 times 500 over 200 is 50 volts. The number 24 wire size affects how much current the windings carry, not the voltage ratio. And remember: a transformer used to step up its input voltage must have more turns of wire on its secondary than on its primary.

onScreen: 150 volt winding: most turns, highest DC resistance
scenes.narration: Here's a power transformer with 1 primary and 3 secondaries, producing 5.0 volts, 12.6 volts and 150 volts, all with similar wire sizes. Which secondary has the highest measured DC resistance? The 150 volt winding. To develop the highest voltage it needs the most turns, and the most turns means the most wire, so it has the most resistance.

callouts.label: Single-phase AC input at 60 Hz
Full-wave output: 2 pulses for each input cycle
Same time base: the output repeats twice as often
Output to input frequency is 2:1, so 120 Hz ripple

scenes.narration: Now a single-phase full-wave rectifier, fed here with 60 hertz AC. A full-wave rectifier turns both halves of each AC cycle into output pulses, so it produces 2 output pulses for each input cycle. On the same time base, the output repeats twice as often as the input. So the ratio of output frequency to input frequency is 2 to 1. A 60 hertz input gives 120 hertz ripple.

params.title: Linear versus switching regulators
rows: Conduction varied in proportion to line or load
On or off; duty cycle set by line or load
An inductor and capacitor smooth the pulses

onScreen: Linear: conduction varied in proportion to line or load
Switching: on or off, duty cycle varied
Inductor and capacitor smooth the pulses
scenes.narration: Voltage regulators come in 2 kinds. In a linear electronic voltage regulator, the conduction of a control element is varied in direct proportion to the line voltage or load current. The pass element acts as a smoothly variable resistance and drops the excess voltage as heat. A switching electronic voltage regulator instead switches the control device on or off, with the duty cycle proportional to the line or load conditions. An inductor and a capacitor then smooth the pulses.

onScreen: Input, output and ground or adjust terminals
scenes.narration: A three-terminal regulator puts a complete regulator in one package. Current enters at the input terminal, flows through the pass element, and leaves at the output terminal. The third terminal is ground, or adjust on adjustable types. Inside, there's also a voltage reference, an error amplifier, and sensing resistors and transistors. The error amplifier compares the sensed output with the reference and controls the pass element. Remember: the 3 terminals are input, output and ground or adjust, not 3 different output voltages.

params.title: The Zener diode: a stable reference

badges.label: Zener diode
badges.note: In breakdown, fed through a current-limiting resistor

badges.label: Pass transistor
badges.note: The Zener only holds the reference steady

onScreen: Pass transistor carries the load current
Ratings: 2.4 volts to 200 volts and above
scenes.narration: In a linear voltage regulator, and in a regulated power supply, the stable reference voltage comes from a Zener diode. It's reverse biased into breakdown through a current-limiting resistor, and in breakdown it holds a nearly constant voltage. The pass transistor only carries the load current; the Zener provides the reference. And Zener diodes are available with voltage ratings from 2.4 volts to 200 volts and above.

params.title: The SCR: silicon-controlled rectifier
items: 3 terminals: anode, cathode and gate
The gate triggers it into conduction
It stays on until the anode current falls below its holding current
Light dimmer: delaying the gate trigger in each half-cycle cuts the lamp's average power

onScreen: Stays on until below holding current
scenes.narration: The SCR, or silicon-controlled rectifier, has 3 terminals: anode, cathode and gate. The gate triggers it into conduction. Once it's on, it stays on until the anode current falls below its holding current. That makes it useful for controlling power. A light-dimming circuit might contain an SCR: delaying its gate trigger within each half-cycle, which is called phase control, reduces the average power to the lamp.

params.title: 2 SCRs sharing a load: inverse parallel

scenes.narration: How might 2 similar SCRs be connected to safely distribute the power load of a circuit? In parallel, reverse polarity, also called inverse parallel. The first SCR handles one half-cycle of the AC, and the second, facing the other way, handles the alternate half-cycle. Each one carries only alternate half-cycles, so the load is shared between them.

params.title: SCR, TRIAC, DIAC and unijunction
rows: 2 complementary SCRs in parallel, common gate
Base 1 and base 2 are not TRIAC terminals

onScreen: TRIAC: 2 SCRs back to back, common gate
scenes.narration: The SCR has anode, cathode and gate, and conducts one way. A TRIAC is fabricated as 2 complementary SCRs in parallel with a common gate terminal. It acts as 2 SCRs back to back, facing in opposite directions and sharing that gate, so it can conduct either way on AC. Its 3 terminals are gate, anode 1 and anode 2, also called main terminals 1 and 2, or MT1 and MT2. A DIAC also conducts both ways, but it has no gate. And base 1 and base 2? Those belong to the unijunction transistor, not the TRIAC.

params.title: Special diodes and their uses
rows: Forward: low RF resistance. Else nearly open
VHF and UHF mixers and detectors
Very fast, low forward voltage, low noise

onScreen: Hot-carrier diode: VHF and UHF mixers and detectors
scenes.narration: Each special diode has a job. One common use for PIN diodes, named for their P-type, intrinsic and N-type layers, is as an RF switch. Forward biased, they present a low RF resistance; with no bias or reverse bias, they're nearly an open circuit. A common use of a hot-carrier, or Schottky, diode is in VHF and UHF mixers and detectors, very high and ultra high frequency, because it switches extremely fast with a low forward voltage and low noise. The tunnel diode amplifies and oscillates. And the varactor diode's capacitance varies with the voltage applied to it.

params.title: Tunnel and varactor diodes up close
items: Tunnel diode: a negative resistance region, where current falls as voltage rises
That lets it both amplify and oscillate, even at microwave frequencies
Varactor: internal capacitance varies with the voltage on its terminals
More reverse voltage widens the depletion layer and lowers the capacitance
So a control voltage can tune a circuit

onScreen: Amplifies and oscillates, even at microwave frequencies
scenes.narration: Let's look closer at 2 of them. The principal characteristic of a tunnel diode is a negative resistance region, where its current decreases as its voltage increases. That negative resistance makes the tunnel diode the special type of diode capable of both amplification and oscillation, even at microwave frequencies. A varactor diode varies its internal capacitance as the voltage applied to its terminals varies. More reverse voltage widens the depletion layer and lowers the capacitance, so a control voltage can tune a circuit.

Structurally, the 2 main categories of semiconductor diodes are junction and point contact. Watch out for the distractors. Electrolytic describes a type of capacitor, and vacuum describes tubes. Neither one is a category of semiconductor diode.

params.title: Whose terminals are these?
rows: Alpha and beta describe its gain

scenes.narration: Transistors next. The 3 terminals of a bipolar transistor are base, collector and emitter. Don't confuse them with other devices' terminals. The unijunction transistor has base 1, base 2 and emitter, and it's used in relaxation oscillators and SCR trigger circuits. Gate, source and drain belong to a FET, a field-effect transistor. And cathode, plate and grid belong to a vacuum tube.

params.title: Alpha and beta: current ratios
steps: α compares I<sub>C</sub> with I<sub>E</sub>: just under 1
β compares I<sub>C</sub> with I<sub>B</sub>: about 20 to several hundred
params.answer: Ratio to base current is beta, not alpha

onScreen: Alpha = change in I sub C / change in I sub E
Beta = change in I sub C / change in I sub B
scenes.narration: 2 current ratios describe a bipolar transistor. Alpha is the change of collector current with respect to emitter current: alpha equals delta I sub C over delta I sub E. Nearly all the emitter current reaches the collector, so alpha is just under 1. Beta is the change of collector current with respect to base current: beta equals delta I sub C over delta I sub B, typically from about 20 to several hundred. So if a question says the ratio to base current, that's beta, not alpha.

params.title: Beta cutoff and saturation
items: Beta cutoff frequency: where the emitter current gain has decreased to 0.707 of maximum
That gain is the common-emitter gain, beta; 0.707 is the −3 dB point
Fully saturated: collector current is at its maximum value
More base current no longer raises it; only supply voltage and load resistance limit it

onScreen: Beta cutoff: emitter current gain down to 0.707 of maximum
Fully saturated: collector current at maximum
Limited by supply voltage and load resistance
scenes.narration: As frequency rises, a transistor's gain falls. The beta cutoff frequency is the frequency at which the emitter current gain, meaning the common-emitter gain, beta, has decreased to 0.707 of its maximum. That's the minus 3 decibel point. At the other extreme, a fully saturated transistor has its collector current at its maximum value. More base current no longer raises it; only the supply voltage and the load resistance limit it.

onScreen: Emitter follower: most current gain, beta plus 1
scenes.narration: Compare the 3 amplifier configurations. A common base amplifier has more voltage gain than common emitter or common collector. Its current gain is just under 1, but it takes the signal in at a very low input impedance and delivers it into a high output impedance. Common emitter falls in between on both counts. An emitter-follower, or common collector, amplifier is the opposite of common base: it has more current gain than common emitter or common base, beta plus 1, while its voltage gain is just under 1.

params.title: Turning on an NPN silicon transistor

callouts.label: Probes across the base-emitter junction
Base at least 0.7 volts positive with respect to the emitter
0.7 volts: the forward voltage a silicon junction needs to conduct
No emitter-collector current: cut off, like an open switch

onScreen: No current: cut off, an open switch
scenes.narration: Put the meter's probes across the base-emitter junction of an NPN silicon transistor, one with N-type, P-type and N-type layers. For current to flow in its emitter-collector junction, the base must be at least 0.7 volts positive with respect to the emitter. That's the forward voltage a silicon junction needs to conduct. Without it, there's no current between emitter and collector, and the transistor is cut off. A cut-off transistor acts like an open switch.

params.title: Junction bias: cutoff, Class A, saturation
rows: Collector current can rise no further

onScreen: Class A: base-emitter forward, collector-base reverse
scenes.narration: Each operating state has its own junction bias. In cutoff, both junctions are reverse biased, and no current flows. When an NPN transistor is operating as a Class A amplifier, the base-emitter junction is forward biased and the collector-base junction is reverse biased. That keeps it in its linear region for the whole cycle. In saturation, the base-emitter junction and the collector-base junction are both forward biased, and collector current can rise no further.

params.title: LEDs: light-emitting diodes
items: Forward bias: electrons recombine with holes and release energy as light
Reverse bias stops the current, so no light
Color is set by the materials used; voltage and current change brightness only
Operating current about 20 mA, also the safe maximum
Hundreds of milliamps would destroy it

onScreen: About 20 mA, also the safe maximum
scenes.narration: An LED needs forward bias to produce luminescence. Electrons crossing the junction recombine with holes and release energy as light. Reverse bias stops the current, so there's no light. The visible color radiated by an LED junction is determined by the materials used to construct the device. Voltage and current change its brightness, not its color. The approximate operating current of a light-emitting diode is 20 milliamps, and 20 milliamps is also the maximum current to safely illuminate it. Hundreds of milliamps would destroy it.

params.title: Protect the LED with a series resistor
steps: Once it conducts, the LED's resistance is very low
The resistor drops the rest of the supply voltage
params.answer: A series resistor must protect every LED

onScreen: LED resistance very low once conducting
scenes.narration: To size the resistor that protects an LED, use R equals V sub supply minus V sub LED, all over I. Once the LED conducts, its resistance is very low, so something must limit the current. The resistor drops the rest of the supply voltage. I is the LED current, typically about 20 milliamps. So a series resistor must be connected to protect an LED.

blocks.label: Light sensor
blocks.note: Open slot: an object can break the beam

onScreen: An object can break the beam
scenes.narration: An LED facing a photodiode in a light-tight enclosure is commonly known as an optoisolator. It's the same idea you met at the start of this lesson: the signal crosses as light, and nothing else connects the 2 sides. An optointerrupter is different. It has an open slot between the LED and the light sensor, so an object passing through the slot can break the beam.

params.title: Junctions, static and CMOS
items: Forward-biased junction: low impedance, small voltage drop. Reverse bias: high impedance
CMOS: complementary metal-oxide semiconductor, P- and N-channel pairs, low static power
FET and CMOS: static charges can puncture the very thin gate oxide
Protection: grounded wrist straps, antistatic mats, conductive packaging

onScreen: FET and CMOS: damaged by static
Wrist straps, antistatic mats, conductive packaging
scenes.narration: A few more devices. A forward-biased diode junction is a low impedance: it conducts heavily with only a small voltage drop. Reverse bias makes it a high impedance. Next, CMOS, which stands for complementary metal-oxide semiconductor. It pairs P-channel and N-channel MOSFETs, metal-oxide semiconductor field-effect transistors, so CMOS logic draws very little static power. FET and CMOS devices need special handling precautions, because they are susceptible to damage from static charges, which can puncture their very thin gate oxide. Grounded wrist straps, antistatic mats and conductive packaging prevent this.

params.title: Quartz crystals and the Pierce oscillator
rows: Applied voltage makes a crystal vibrate
Quartz crystal in feedback path sets frequency
An LC tank sets the frequency instead

onScreen: Piezoelectric effect: voltage makes a crystal vibrate
Pierce oscillator: quartz crystal in the feedback path
scenes.narration: The piezoelectric effect is mechanical vibration of a crystal by the application of a voltage. It works the other way too: squeezing the crystal produces a voltage in return. You'll find a quartz crystal in the Pierce oscillator, where it sits in the feedback path and sets the frequency. Hartley and Colpitts oscillators set their frequency with an L C tank, a coil and a capacitor, instead.

params.title: The relay: a remotely controlled switch

onScreen: Separate set of contacts opens or closes
scenes.narration: Finally, the electrical relay. A relay is a remotely controlled switching device. A small current flows through its electromagnet coil. The coil's magnetic pull opens or closes a separate set of contacts, and those contacts switch a different circuit. So a small control signal in one place can switch a circuit somewhere else.
